rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained components. The elution window will guide subsequent narrowing and slope or temperature tests.

Injection 1 already achieved the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Halve the gradient duration to seek a shorter fully resolved separation and measure how the critical pair responds to slope.
The critical pair responds strongly to gradient slope. Increase tG one grid step from the unresolved 6-minute method to seek full resolution while remaining substantially faster than injection 1.
Injection 3 retains maximum CRF with a shorter separation. Raise temperature while keeping the gradient fixed to test whether faster elution preserves the critical pair’s resolution.

Trim the gradient window and shorten tG while keeping nearly the same slope as injection 4. Starting below the estimated first-peak elution composition should reduce initial waiting time while testing whether full resolution is preserved.

Narrow the window further while retaining a slightly shallower slope than injection 5 to protect the critical pair. This should shorten the separation, with the main risk being compression of the first two peaks.

Lower phi1 one grid step to make the gradient slightly shallower and recover the critical pair’s small resolution deficit. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, potentially preserving full resolution in less time than injection 5.
Test whether a 5 °C increase rescues the marginal middle pair in injection 6 while shortening retention. Monitor the first pair closely, since higher temperature previously reduced its separation.

Raise the starting organic fraction to shorten retention, while using a shallower gradient to protect the middle pair. Lower temperature should help preserve separation of the early pair, which became limiting at 55 °C.

Raise temperature one step from injection 9 to improve the marginal middle pair and shorten the separation. The early pair’s resolution of 2.70 provides some margin for the expected loss at higher temperature.

Retain injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved method so far, and test a much steeper gradient for a potentially faster separation with changed elution order. The middle pair may separate again beyond its co-elution region, although other pairs could become compressed.

Test a colder, higher-starting-organic method to shift selectivity in the fast-gradient regime. Lower temperature should help retain and separate the early compounds while probing whether the middle pair can resolve in reversed order.

Explore a higher starting organic fraction with a much shallower gradient to shift the middle-pair selectivity rather than merely compress it. Low temperature should help retain the early compounds, though their proximity to the dead time is the main risk.

Maximum CRF is already secured; test a method with more resolution margin than the fastest qualifying run. Lowering the starting fraction while retaining injection 7’s slope should improve the early and middle pairs, with all peaks still expected well before 10 minutes.

Lower the starting organic fraction relative to injection 8 to improve early-pair retention and separation at 55 °C. The steeper gradient should keep the run short while testing whether the middle pair retains sufficient resolution.

Test a short, shallow gradient followed by a hold to preserve middle-pair resolution while ending the programmed gradient earlier. The final compound will likely elute during the hold, so its retention will determine whether this offers any practical time advantage over injection 10.

Test whether a higher starting fraction can be balanced by a shallower slope to retain full resolution. Use 45 °C to protect the early pair, and compare the resulting separation time with injection 10, the fastest maximum-CRF method so far.

Refine around injection 10 with a slightly shallower gradient to increase its narrow middle-pair resolution margin. This should preserve maximum CRF with only a small retention-time increase, providing a more forgiving alternative to the fastest qualifying method.

Use a slope between injections 6 and 7 to target the shortest fully resolved separation at phi0 = 0.20. This should recover the small resolution deficit of injection 6 while retaining more early-pair separation than injection 10.

Preserve injection 16’s initial composition and slope but extend the gradient beyond its low-organic hold. This should retain its resolution margin while bringing the last compound out earlier, yielding another maximum-CRF candidate.
Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 10 to locate the speed limit near the fastest fully resolved method. The middle pair may fall just below R = 1.5; retain injection 10 if that occurs.

The faster neighboring slopes now bracket the middle-pair resolution limit. Test a shallower gradient at the better-retained starting composition to obtain a maximum-CRF alternative with more resolution margin while keeping the last peak near four minutes.

Test temperature sensitivity around injection 22, which achieved maximum CRF with substantial resolution margin. Cooling one step should improve the early pair while checking that the middle pair remains fully resolved, providing a robust alternative to the faster injection 10.

Steepen injection 23 by raising phi1 one step to shorten elution while using its middle-pair resolution margin. This also tests whether injection 7’s maximum CRF is preserved at a temperature 5 °C lower.

Use the final injection to interpolate between the fully resolved slopes of injections 7 and 22, targeting maximum CRF with useful resolution margin. Injection 10 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method, with the last peak at 3.40 minutes.
